course: Convert a Car Engine to an Irrigation Water Pump

lessons.title: Why a Pump Engine Overheats Faster Than a Car Engine
lessons.body: When a car engine drives a pump, it runs at a steady, high load for hours, often in the hot sun. In a car, the engine gets air flow from the vehicle's motion, but a stationary pump engine sits still. The radiator relies only on the fan, and if that fan is weak or missing, heat builds up fast. Also, pump engines often run at 1500-1800 RPM continuously, which is higher than idle but lower than highway speeds, so the water pump may turn slower than designed. In Africa, ambient temperatures can exceed 40Ã‚Â°C, and dusty air clogs the radiator fins. Without proper cooling, the engine will overheat within 20-30 minutes, leading to cracked heads, blown gaskets, and seized pistons. You must adapt the cooling system to handle this constant heavy load. This module shows you how to modify the radiator, fan, and coolant flow to keep the engine at 80-90Ã‚Â°C, the safe operating range. We'll cover fan selection, radiator cleaning, thermostat removal, and adding a water tank. By the end, you'll be able to run your pump for 8 hours straight without overheating.

lessons.title: Removing the Thermostat and Restricting Bypass
lessons.body: In a car, the thermostat stays closed until the engine warms up, then opens to let coolant flow to the radiator. For a pump engine, you want full coolant flow all the time, because the engine is always under load. Remove the thermostat completely. On most engines, it's located in a housing where the upper radiator hose connects to the engine block. Unbolt the housing (usually two 12mm bolts), take out the thermostat, and either leave it out or install a blanking sleeve. But be careful: some engines have a bypass hose that lets coolant circulate through the block without going to the radiator. If you remove the thermostat, too much coolant may bypass the radiator, causing overheating. You need to block that bypass. Look for a small hose (about 20mm diameter) running from the water pump to the intake manifold or cylinder head. Plug it with a brass cap or a bolt clamped inside the hose. Alternatively, some thermostats have a bypass block built in; if you remove it, you must restrict the bypass. A simple method is to insert a metal plate with a 5mm hole in the bypass line. This allows some flow for warm-up but forces most coolant through the radiator. Test by running the engine and feeling the upper hose; it should get hot quickly. If it stays cold, coolant isn't flowing. Always use new gaskets and sealant when reassembling.

lessons.title: Upgrading the Radiator and Fan for Stationary Use
lessons.body: The original car radiator may be too small for continuous pump duty. If your engine is from a small car (1.0-1.6L), the radiator might handle it, but for larger engines (2.0L and above), you need a bigger radiator. Visit a scrapyard and find a radiator from a truck or a larger car, like a Toyota Hilux or Nissan Hardbody. Ensure it has similar hose connection sizes (usually 32mm and 38mm). If you can't find one, you can add a second radiator in parallel, but that's complex. More important is the fan. A mechanical fan driven by the water pump belt is often inadequate when stationary. Install an electric fan from a car air conditioner or a universal 12V fan. Mount it on the radiator with a shroud to pull air through the entire core. A 16-inch fan pulling 2000 CFM is good for most conversions. Wire it to a relay and a manual switch, or better, a thermostatic switch that turns on at 85Ã‚Â°C. Also, clean the radiator fins with a soft brush and compressed air; dust and mud block airflow. In dusty conditions, consider adding a screen in front of the radiator. Finally, ensure the radiator cap holds pressure: a 0.9 bar cap raises the boiling point to about 120Ã‚Â°C, which helps prevent boil-over.

lessons.title: Adding a Water Tank and Overflow System
lessons.body: A car's cooling system is sealed and uses a small overflow bottle. For a pump engine, you need a larger reserve because you'll be running for hours and may lose coolant through minor leaks or evaporation. Get a 20-liter plastic jerrycan or a metal tank. Connect it to the radiator overflow port with a hose. The tank should have a vent to atmosphere and a pickup tube that reaches the bottom. When the engine cools, coolant is sucked back into the radiator. This is called a recovery system. Make sure the radiator cap is a recovery type (it has a rubber seal at the top). If you use a standard cap, it won't suck back. Also, check for leaks regularly. A small leak can drop the coolant level and cause overheating. Use a 50/50 mix of antifreeze and water. Antifreeze raises the boiling point and prevents corrosion, which is important in older engines. In areas where water is hard, use distilled water if possible. If you can't get antifreeze, use clean rainwater and add a corrosion inhibitor. Never use plain borehole water without treatment; minerals will clog the radiator. Check the coolant level every morning before starting. Top up to the cold mark on the tank. During operation, watch the temperature gauge; if it climbs above 95Ã‚Â°C, stop and check for problems.

lessons.title: Flushing and Cleaning the Cooling System
lessons.body: A used car engine likely has rust, scale, and sludge in the cooling passages. Before you run your pump, flush the system thoroughly. Start by draining the old coolant. Open the drain plug at the bottom of the radiator and the block drain (often a 14mm bolt on the side of the engine block). Collect the old coolant in a pan; it's toxic, so dispose of it properly. Then fill the system with clean water and a flushing chemical, like a citric acid flush or a commercial radiator cleaner. Run the engine for 15 minutes with the radiator cap off, heater on full (if you have one), and then drain. Repeat until the water comes out clear. For heavy rust, you may need to remove the radiator and take it to a radiator shop for a professional rodding. If that's not possible, you can backflush with a garden hose: disconnect the upper hose and force water through the radiator from the bottom outlet. Also, remove the water pump and inspect the impeller; if it's corroded or broken, replace it. A new water pump costs about $30-50 and is worth it. Check all hoses for cracks and soft spots; replace any that are questionable. Use new hose clamps. After flushing, fill with a 50/50 mix of ethylene glycol antifreeze and clean water. Bleed air from the system by running the engine with the cap off until the thermostat opens (but remember, you removed it, so just run until no bubbles appear). Top up and close.

lessons.title: Monitoring Temperature and Preventing Overheat
lessons.body: You need to know the engine temperature at all times. Install a mechanical or electric temperature gauge if your engine doesn't have one. The sensor goes into the cylinder head or thermostat housing. A good gauge has numbers, not just a red light. Normal operating temperature is 80-90Ã‚Â°C. If it reaches 100Ã‚Â°C, stop the engine and let it cool. Common causes of overheating in pump engines: a slipping fan belt (check tension, should deflect 10-15mm), a stuck closed thermostat (but you removed it), a clogged radiator, a failed water pump, or low coolant. Always carry spare coolant and a spare fan belt. In hot climates, consider adding a second electric fan or a larger radiator. You can also reduce load by lowering pump speed if possible. Use a laser thermometer to check temperatures at the radiator inlet and outlet; the difference should be about 10Ã‚Â°C. If the outlet is much cooler, the radiator is working. If both are hot, the radiator is not dissipating heat. Also, listen for the fan running; if it's not, check the fuse and relay. Keep the radiator fins clean by blowing them out with compressed air every week. Never remove the radiator cap while the engine is hot; steam and boiling water can burn you. Let it cool for at least 30 minutes. By following these steps, your pump engine will run reliably for many seasons.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cooling System Specifications, Temperature Limits and Maintenance Schedule

This Practical Reference consolidates the hard numbers you need when converting a car engine into a stationary irrigation pump. Unlike a vehicle, a stationary engine has no ram airflow, runs at constant load for hours, and often sits in 35â42 Â°C ambient heat. The cooling system therefore becomes the single most important determinant of engine life, fuel efficiency per cubic metre of water lifted, and the reliability your farm business depends on. Use the tables, diagram and checklist below as your workshop reference sheet. Print it, laminate it, and keep it in the pump house.

Table 1: Coolant Temperature and Pressure Operating Limits

Parameter Normal Operating Range Warning Threshold Action Required
Coolant temperature (pressurised) 80â95 Â°C Above 100 Â°C Stop engine, allow cooling, inspect thermostat and fan
Coolant temperature (open, unpressurised) 75â88 Â°C Above 90 Â°C Reduce load, check coolant level
Radiator cap pressure rating 0.9â1.1 bar (13â16 psi) Below 0.7 bar Replace cap â weak cap lowers boiling point
Coolant boiling point (50% glycol, 1 bar cap) ~125 Â°C â Use glycol mix where ambient exceeds 40 Â°C
Oil temperature (sump) 90â110 Â°C Above 120 Â°C Check oil cooler, reduce continuous load
Intake air temperature (ambient +) Ambient +10 to +25 Â°C Above ambient +40 Â°C Reposition air intake away from radiator discharge

Sources: Values compiled from FAO Land and Water Division pump-set installation guidance; Caterpillar/Perkins stationary engine operation manuals; and standard automotive cooling system engineering practice (SAE J814). Field adjustment recommended for African ambient conditions of 35â42 Â°C.

Table 2: Coolant Mixture Ratios and Maintenance Intervals

Item Specification / Ratio Service Interval Notes for African Conditions
Ethylene glycol concentration 40â50% glycol : 50â60% water Check monthly; replace every 24 months 50% mix protects to â37 Â°C and raises boiling point
Distilled / soft water 100% â avoid hard borehole water Every top-up Hard water scales radiator cores within 6â12 months
Coolant pH 7.5â11.0 Every 6 months Acidic coolant corrodes aluminium heads
Radiator core external cleaning Compressed air or low-pressure water Weekly in dusty conditions Dust blocks fins; reduces heat rejection by up to 40%
Coolant full flush Drain, flush, refill Every 12â24 months More frequent if borehole water used
Fan belt tension 10â15 mm deflection at mid-span Weekly Slipping belt = overheating within 20 minutes
Thermostat function test Opens at rated temp (typically 82 Â°C) Every 12 months Test in hot water before refitting
Hose and clamp inspection No cracks, no swelling Monthly UV and heat degrade rubber rapidly in the tropics

Sources: ILRI smallholder mechanisation briefs; FAO Operation and Maintenance of Small Irrigation Schemes; Perkins and Kubota stationary engine service schedules.

â  SAFETY WARNING â PRESSURISED HOT COOLANT

Never open a radiator cap while the engine is hot. Pressurised coolant at 90â100 Â°C will flash to steam and cause severe scalding burns to the face, arms and torso. Allow the engine to cool for at least 30 minutes before removing the cap, and cover the cap with a thick cloth while turning it to the first stop to release residual pressure slowly. Ethylene glycol is toxic if swallowed â store coolant in clearly labelled containers away from children, livestock and drinking water sources. If coolant is swallowed, seek medical attention immediately and contact your nearest poison information centre. Dispose of used coolant at an approved hazardous waste facility; never pour it onto soil or into irrigation channels.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check coolant level daily before starting â top up only when the engine is cold, using the correct glycol mix.
  2. Confirm the thermostat is fitted and functioning â never run permanently without one; it regulates warm-up and flow.
  3. Verify the bypass orifice is 5â8 mm â too large wastes cooling capacity, too small causes hot spots.
  4. Inspect the radiator fins weekly â blow out dust with compressed air; a blocked core is the number one cause of pump-set overheating.
  5. Check fan belt tension and fan operation â the electric fan must cut in automatically; test the switch monthly.
  6. Monitor the temperature gauge continuously â investigate any reading above 95 Â°C within two minutes.
  7. Inspect hoses, clamps and the expansion tank monthly for cracks, swelling or leaks.
  8. Record every top-up and flush in a logbook â unexplained coolant loss signals a head gasket or water pump failure.

Further Reading

  • FAO Land and Water Division â Irrigation and Pumping Resources (free technical guides on small-scale pumping systems).
  • ILRI â Smallholder Mechanisation and Livestock Water Publications (open-access briefs on engine-driven water lifting in East Africa).
  • WHO â Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (relevant where pump coolant or fuel may contaminate irrigation and drinking water).
  • Penn State Extension â Agricultural and Biological Engineering (free articles on engine maintenance and irrigation pump operation).
  • USDA Agricultural Research Service â Cropping Systems and Water Quality (research on irrigation efficiency and pump performance).

Business note: A pump set that overheats once a week costs you roughly 3â5 hours of irrigation time, which in a 2-hectare vegetable operation can translate to 20â30% yield loss during a dry spell. Treat the cooling system as a profit centre, not a maintenance nuisance. A disciplined weekly 15-minute inspection routine is the cheapest insurance your irrigation business can buy.

quiz.q: Why does a pump engine overheat faster than a car engine?
options: A) It runs at higher RPM
B) It lacks airflow from vehicle motion
D) It has a smaller radiator
quiz.explanation: A stationary pump engine does not get ram air like a moving car, so it relies solely on the fan for cooling.

quiz.q: What is the safe operating temperature range for a converted pump engine?
quiz.explanation: Most engines are designed to run efficiently between 80Ã‚Â°C and 90Ã‚Â°C; higher temperatures risk damage.

quiz.q: What should you do with the thermostat when converting to a pump engine?
options: D) Replace it with a higher temperature one
quiz.explanation: Removing the thermostat ensures full coolant flow to the radiator at all times, which is needed for continuous heavy load.

quiz.q: Why must you restrict the bypass hose when removing the thermostat?
options: A) To increase coolant flow to the radiator
B) To prevent coolant from bypassing the radiator
C) To raise the engine temperature
D) To reduce pressure in the system
quiz.explanation: Without restriction, too much coolant would circulate through the block and not enough would go to the radiator, causing overheating.

quiz.q: What size hole is recommended in a bypass restriction plate?
quiz.explanation: A 5mm hole allows some warm-up flow but forces most coolant through the radiator.

quiz.q: What is a sign that coolant is not flowing through the radiator after removing the thermostat?
options: A) The upper hose stays cold
B) The engine runs too cool
quiz.explanation: If the upper hose remains cold, coolant is not circulating through the radiator, indicating a blockage or air lock.

quiz.q: When upgrading the radiator for a pump engine, what should you look for at a scrapyard?
options: A) A radiator from a small car
B) A radiator from a truck or larger car
C) A radiator with plastic tanks
D) A radiator with no cap
quiz.explanation: Truck or larger car radiators have more cooling capacity, which is needed for continuous pump duty.

quiz.q: What is the recommended CFM for an electric fan on a converted pump engine?
quiz.explanation: A 16-inch fan pulling about 2000 CFM is sufficient for most conversions to ensure adequate airflow.

quiz.q: Why is a shroud important when mounting an electric fan?
options: B) It pulls air through the entire radiator core
quiz.explanation: A shroud directs airflow across the whole radiator, improving cooling efficiency.

quiz.q: What pressure cap is recommended for a pump engine cooling system?
quiz.explanation: A 0.9 bar cap raises the boiling point to about 120Ã‚Â°C, helping prevent boil-over.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding a water tank to the cooling system?
options: B) To act as a coolant reservoir
C) To cool the engine oil
quiz.explanation: A larger reservoir ensures there is enough coolant to compensate for minor losses and expansion.

quiz.q: What type of radiator cap is needed for a coolant recovery system?
options: B) A recovery cap with a rubber seal
C) A cap with no spring
D) A cap with a lever
quiz.explanation: A recovery cap allows coolant to be drawn back from the overflow tank when the engine cools.

quiz.q: What is the correct mixing ratio for antifreeze and water?
quiz.explanation: A 50/50 mix provides the best balance of freeze protection, boil-over protection, and corrosion inhibition.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using plain borehole water in the cooling system?
options: B) It contains minerals that can clog the radiator
quiz.explanation: Hard water leaves scale deposits that reduce heat transfer and can block passages.

quiz.q: What should you do before flushing the cooling system?
options: A) Run the engine until hot
quiz.explanation: Draining the old coolant first prevents mixing with the flushing solution and allows proper disposal.

quiz.q: Where is the block drain plug typically located?
options: B) On the side of the engine block
quiz.explanation: The block drain is usually a bolt on the side of the engine block, used to drain coolant from the block.

quiz.q: What is a sign that the water pump impeller may be damaged?
options: A) The engine runs too cool
B) Coolant flows poorly even after flushing
quiz.explanation: A damaged impeller cannot circulate coolant effectively, leading to poor flow and overheating.

quiz.q: Why is it important to bleed air from the cooling system?
options: A) Air pockets can cause hot spots and overheating
quiz.explanation: Air trapped in the system can create steam pockets that prevent proper coolant flow and cause localized overheating.

quiz.q: What is the normal operating temperature for a pump engine?
quiz.explanation: 80-90Ã‚Â°C is the efficient and safe operating range for most engines.

quiz.q: What should you do if the temperature gauge reaches 100Ã‚Â°C?
options: B) Stop the engine and let it cool
quiz.explanation: At 100Ã‚Â°C, the engine is overheating; stopping and cooling prevents damage.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of overheating in a pump engine?
quiz.explanation: A slipping fan belt reduces water pump and fan speed, leading to poor cooling.

quiz.q: How much should a fan belt deflect when pressed?
quiz.explanation: A deflection of 10-15mm indicates correct tension; too loose slips, too tight damages bearings.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to check radiator inlet and outlet temperatures?
quiz.explanation: A laser thermometer allows non-contact temperature measurement to assess radiator performance.

quiz.q: What should the temperature difference between radiator inlet and outlet be?
quiz.explanation: A drop of about 10Ã‚Â°C indicates the radiator is dissipating heat properly.

quiz.q: Why should you never remove the radiator cap while the engine is hot?
options: A) It may damage the cap
B) Steam and boiling water can burn you
C) It will cause an air lock
D) It will void the warranty
quiz.explanation: The system is under pressure and hot; opening the cap can release scalding steam and coolant.

quiz.q: How often should you clean the radiator fins in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning prevents dust and mud from blocking airflow, which is critical in dusty environments.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using antifreeze in a hot climate?
options: A) It raises the boiling point
B) It lowers the freezing point
quiz.explanation: Antifreeze raises the boiling point of coolant, helping prevent boil-over in hot conditions.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a cracked hose?
quiz.explanation: A cracked hose can burst under pressure; replacing it is the only safe solution.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a recovery tank vent?
options: A) To allow air to escape and enter as coolant expands and contracts
quiz.explanation: The vent allows atmospheric pressure to act on the coolant, enabling it to be drawn back into the radiator.

quiz.q: What should you do if the electric fan does not come on?
options: A) Check the fuse and relay
quiz.explanation: A blown fuse or faulty relay is a common cause of fan failure; check those first.
